title: High Crime
full_review:
A devoted wife jumps into the fray when her husband is accused of murdering foreign civilians while in the Marines in the muddled courtroom drama, "High Crimes" (20th Century Fox).

Director Carl Franklin's sleek visuals never disappoint but the narrative ultimately does. The storyline is engrossing with its undercurrent of danger and suspense -- only to wind up in such a way little makes sense when you reflect on who did what and why, and how for that matter. It's possible to enjoy the movie if you just let it wash over you, but once you try to connect the dots the whole plot collapses in a senseless finale of unanswered questions.

But that's not to say that Morgan Freeman and Ashley Judd don't have a really nice on-screen chemistry together. Previously paired in "Kiss the Girls," by now they seem a smart and comfortable fit as two lawyers trying to save her husband (Jim Caviezel) who is on trial by the military for a capitol crime.

As the movie begins Claire (Judd) and Tom (Caviezel) are living in high style in Marin County although we have no idea what he does for a living. Not that it matters much since he is soon arrested, accused of killing innocent villagers in El Salvador -- and admits to Claire he did take on a new identity to escape the charges he denies as utterly false. Unfamiliar with military courtroom procedure, Claire enlists disgraced ex-Marine attorney Charlie Grimes (Freeman) to help in her husband's defense since the assigned defense lawyer Lt. Embrey (Adam Scott) is inexperienced and intimidated by the big guns the on the prosecution side.

Thus begins a tale of secrets, cover ups, spying and betrayals that is interesting to follow down its dark alleyways, but when dawn breaks there is little light to be had for inquiring minds. Lest logic raise its unwanted head the characters are given texture: Grimes is a recovering alcoholic willing to end his sobriety to find incriminating evidence; Claire may not be able to sustain her pregnancy, and her scatterbrained sister (Amanda Peet in a nearly pointless role) seduces Lt. Embrey, who may or may not be a mole for the Marines.

Various military types threaten, cajole and close ranks, making Claire's job of getting to the truth all the harder. Her husband fears for her life and always has tears at the ready when she asks hard questions about why he never confided in her.

Well acted and nicely paced, there are enough red herrings to hold interest, with the occasional flashback to the mass murder in the village years earlier. But one has to take everything at face value and not question the loose ends to accept "High Crimes" as high drama rather than the murky melodrama it becomes.

Due to intermittent violence and a brief sexual situation, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
